case_study_insert.main_stem: Tarnfield School Furniture (TSF) is a private limited company in the furniture manufacturing sector, producing wooden school desks, chairs and library shelving for primary schools and academies, with a workforce of 52. Founded in 2002 by Colin Tarnfield, it operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. TSF plans to invest $780,000 in a new CNC routing and spray-finishing line, financed by $500,000 hire purchase and $280,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $276,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.80 a unit and a selling price of $34.80, and produces 46,000 units a year. TSF faces rising customer complaints about wobbly chair legs and an emerging skills gap in spray finishing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Advertisement Extract — Furniture Trade Journal (March 2025): 'Tarnfield School Furniture: the Oakfield range — desk and chair sets at $34.80 a unit, 10% introductory discount on orders over 500 units, free toolkit and assembly guide, delivery within 21 days of order, 5-year frame guarantee.' The advert generated 38 enquiries in its first fortnight. The current order book covers 9,200 units of the Oakfield range. 31 of 52 staff have trained on the spray-finishing booth; the off-the-job spray course at the furniture college costs $680 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tarnfield School Furniture as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with hire purchase agreements and variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 4.9% from $12.30 to $12.90 per hour from April 2026. (3) Timber and MDF input costs have risen 11.3% year-on-year and manufacturing input-cost inflation is running at 6.5%, while local authority capital spending on school refurbishment grew 3.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: TSF plans to finance part of its new CNC and spray-finishing line with hire purchase. Explain two advantages for TSF of hire purchase instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Hire purchase spreads the $500,000 cost of the CNC routing and spray-finishing line over fixed monthly instalments matched to the revenue the Oakfield range generates, so TSF does not need to find a large lump sum or charge its balance sheet with a single huge debt. Interest is built into the agreement, ownership of the equipment passes to TSF after the final payment, and the monthly schedule is predictable for cash planning.

Point 2: Hire purchase secures the machinery against itself — the lender's security is the CNC line, not TSF's factory or Colin Tarnfield's personal guarantees — so the family's wider assets are protected if school contracts slow. Crucially, it preserves TSF's retained profit ($280,000 contribution) as working capital for timber purchases while timber input costs rise 11.3%, and avoids the penalty structures and covenants that often accompany small-business bank loans; if a better line arrives, TSF can simply let the agreement lapse at the end rather than refinance.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Tarnfield School Furniture and its CNC and spray-finishing expansion.

questions.question_text: TSF is promoting its Oakfield range to schools nationwide. Consider direct-mail catalogues to head teachers, exhibiting at the National Education Resources Show, or social media advertising aimed at school business managers. Which should TSF choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Direct-mail catalogues to head teachers: A full-colour Oakfield catalogue mailed to every primary school and academy on TSF's list costs only a few dollars per pack including postage, lands directly on the desk of the person who signs the furniture order, and led to 38 enquiries in a fortnight from the single trade-journal advert, suggesting print formats work. Weaknesses are low response rates, no guarantee of budget timing, and it ignores academy trusts that procure centrally through business managers rather than head teachers.

Exhibiting at the National Education Resources Show: A stand reaches thousands of head teachers and business managers in two days, with real desks and chairs to sit on — instant credibility for a furniture maker whose current weakness is complaints about wobbly chair legs. Cost of space, travel and samples absorbs a sizeable slice of the $780,000 expansion budget, and it consumes Colin Tarnfield's time away from the factory, but a single signed academy-trust deal could cover the whole cost many times over.

Social media advertising aimed at school business managers: Targeted campaigns on LinkedIn and education forums cost a modest four-figure sum each month, are precisely measurable, and suit a younger generation of academy business managers who specify furniture digitally. However, the buying cycle is long and cautious, and trust in an unfamiliar manufacturer advertising online may be low compared with a guaranteed 5-year frame.

Recommendation: TSF should choose the National Education Resources Show. Selling school furniture is a considered, high-ticket, relationship purchase; demonstrating build quality face-to-face directly counters the wobbly-chair complaint problem and can produce multi-academy-trust framework agreements worth tens of thousands of units. Direct mail is rejected as too low-yield for the premium the Oakfield range carries; social media is rejected as too weak a trust builder for a $34.80-a-unit contract sale, though it should be used as a cheap follow-up channel after the show.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TSF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of TSF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why direct mail and social media are rejected as the lead channel.

questions.question_text: TSF uses a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for TSF of laissez-faire leadership for its skilled furniture makers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives TSF's experienced joiners and finishers — 31 of whom already know the spray booth — freedom to set their own pace and methods within quality standards. Craft work such as oak-veneer desks benefits from this autonomy, because skilled makers spot grain and joint defects by eye faster than any inspector, raising quality without supervisory cost.

Point 2: Laissez-faire leadership frees Colin Tarnfield to focus on sales and the 9,200-unit order book rather than daily supervision. In a flat structure with 52 employees and no middle managers, delegation avoids bottlenecks, develops senior makers into informal leaders, and keeps decisions fast on the floor. The risk, visible in the wobbly-chair complaints and the spray-finishing skills gap, is that laissez-faire slides into neglect; benefits therefore depend on keeping clear written quality standards and reviewing output weekly. Used well, it also lets senior makers flag suspect batches to Colin Tarnfield before spraying and packing, cutting the rework that currently erodes the margin on the advertised 10% introductory discount.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TSF's complaints, order book and structure.

questions.question_text: TSF must re-motivate its finishing team, whose quality is slipping. Consider introducing a performance-related bonus, or job enrichment through rotation between CNC, assembly and finishing. Which should TSF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Performance-related bonus: A bonus paid on defect-free output, tied to a measurable quality threshold, directly rewards what TSF needs most: fewer wobbly chair legs. It is measurable, cheap to administer on a piece-rate finishing team, easily understood by 52 workshop staff, and self-funding if scrap and rework fall. Risks are that finishers rush to hit numbers (worsening defects), quality-chasing becomes gamed, and it treats symptoms of demotivation rather than the underlying boredom and skills gap.

Job enrichment through rotation (CNC, assembly, finishing): Rotation satisfies Herzberg's motivator needs — variety, growth and responsibility — and attacks the root cause: finishers who only spray all day become disengaged and careless. It also cross-trains the 21 untrained staff for the new CNC routing and spray line, increases flexibility across the whole factory, and suits a flat, laissez-faire culture better than a pay-only lever. Drawbacks are slower task mastery, more set-up time, and short-term dips in finishing throughput while people learn.

Decision: TSF should choose job enrichment through rotation, introduced gradually over one term with bonus pilots retained for the spray-booth team. Rotation builds genuine, lasting competence in the $780,000 CNC and spray-finishing line, closes the skills gap identified in the training analysis, and fits the flat laissez-faire ethos; a pure performance bonus is rejected because it pays for speed rather than craft and would likely widen the gap between fast joiners and struggling finishers. A modest bonus can be bolted on later as a reinforcing signal once rotation beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two motivation approaches with limited application to TSF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of financial and non-financial motivation in the context of TSF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of TSF with a well-justified decision covering cost, skills development, quality and culture.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TSF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $276,000 ÷ ($34.80 − $22.80) = $276,000 ÷ $12.00 = 23,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 23,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $34.80 − $22.80 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TSF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Management can compare the 23,000-unit break-even output with current production of 46,000 units to confirm the Oakfield range is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 23,000 units, before committing to the full $780,000 CNC and spray-finishing line.
2. A contribution per unit of $12.00 lets TSF model the effect of its advertised 10% introductory discount on orders over 500 units: the discounted price would be $31.32, cutting contribution to $8.52, so managers can judge whether large-volume orders still cover the $276,000 fixed costs.
3. Fixed costs of $276,000 combined with the $12.00 contribution inform the hire purchase feasibility test on the $500,000 agreement, showing how many units beyond break-even are needed to service the monthly instalments alongside day-to-day timber purchases.
4. Unit cost data ($276,000 ÷ 46,000 units + $22.80 = $28.80) lets managers benchmark the Oakfield range against the advertised $34.80 price, target the wobbly-chair complaint rate for reduction, and renegotiate the $22.80 variable cost with timber and MDF suppliers amid 11.3% input-cost inflation; labour productivity of about 885 units per worker (46,000 ÷ 52) frames realistic output targets for the enlarged team.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 23,000 units ($276,000 ÷ $12.00) | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 ($34.80 − $22.80) | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 23,000 units against 46,000-unit output; modelling the advertised 10% introductory discount on $34.80 Oakfield sets (to $31.32, contribution $8.52) against $276,000 fixed costs; feasibility check for the $500,000 hire purchase agreement funding the $780,000 CNC and spray-finishing line; unit-cost benchmarking at $28.80 against the wobbly-chair complaint problem and 11.3% timber inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TSF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TSF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.54 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.62 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.00 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.18 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $210,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $430,000; 2025 current assets = $120,000 + $230,000 + $95,000 = $445,000. 2024: $430,000 ÷ $280,000 = 1.54; 2025: $445,000 ÷ $275,000 = 1.62. For the stricter measure, 2024: ($430,000 − $150,000) ÷ $280,000 = $280,000 ÷ $280,000 = 1.00; 2025: ($445,000 − $120,000) ÷ $275,000 = $325,000 ÷ $275,000 = 1.18.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved, and in good quality. Inventories were deliberately run down from $150,000 to $120,000 — a positive signal for a furniture maker vulnerable to fashion and specification drift — while cash rose from $70,000 to $95,000. Current liabilities even fell slightly from $280,000 to $275,000, so the stronger coverage is not borrowed. The acid test crossing from exactly 1.00 to 1.18 means TSF can now meet every short-term debt without selling desks and chairs — a real strengthening of resilience while $500,000 of hire purchase instalments accrue. However, trade receivables crept up from $210,000 to $230,000, and many school customers pay on 30-60 day terms; if academy accounts go quiet over the summer, cash could tighten quickly.

Conclusion: TSF's financial position has improved. Liquidity strengthened on both measures and the improvement is driven by leaner stock and higher cash, not by rising liabilities. TSF should keep tightening receivables collection from academies, hold the inventory discipline that is freeing up cash, and use the strengthened headroom to complete the spray-finishing training before adding the next hire purchase tranche.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TSF's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TSF of launching a direct-to-school e-commerce website for the Oakfield range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A direct-to-school e-commerce website would let academy business managers configure Oakfield desk and chair sets, place orders and track deliveries without phoning Tarnfield, cutting administration cost per order and capturing the digital-first procurement trend. With 38 enquiries from a single print advert, converting even part of that interest online protects TSF's 46,000-unit output, improves cash collection (schools pay up front or on delivery), and opens sales to regions TSF's direct reps never visit.

Disadvantage: Building and maintaining a secure site, photography, payment processing and order tracking could cost tens of thousands of dollars before the first sale, and schools rarely buy furniture impulsively — a website will not fix the trust deficit behind the wobbly-chair complaints. Poor fulfilment or stockouts online would scale reputational damage across the country far faster than the current regional word-of-mouth, and laissez-faire leadership means no one currently owns the website's daily order queue, risking abandoned carts and missed deliveries.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to TSF's order book, complaints and channel strategy.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 4.9% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in timber input costs will affect TSF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise to 4.75%: TSF's $500,000 hire purchase agreement, which embeds interest, will become more expensive to renew, and any short-term borrowing renewed between school payment cycles also costs more. Roughly 0.75% on the outstanding hire purchase balance is about $3,000-$4,000 a year of additional finance cost — noticeable against TSF's improved but still modest $95,000 cash, though it is the smallest of the three pressures.

Minimum wage increase of 4.9% to $12.90: TSF's 52 workers in cutting, assembly and finishing are heavily hand-intensive. If average earnings are near $12.90 an hour for 2,080 hours, each worker adds about $1,250 a year, or around $65,000 across the workforce — a serious but partly absorbable rise, given flat-structure productivity gains from CNC routing and the 3.2% growth in local authority school-refurbishment spending supporting demand.

Timber and MDF input cost inflation of 11.3%: TSF's $22.80 variable cost is dominated by timber; a 11.3% rise on the wood component (roughly $13-$14 per unit) adds about $1.50-$1.58 per set. Across 46,000 units that is roughly $68,000-$73,000 a year, compressing contribution per unit from $12.00 toward $10.40-$10.50 and eroding the margin behind the Oakfield launch before the $780,000 CNC line is fully paid for.

Conclusion: The 11.3% timber input-cost inflation will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 46,000 units (~$68,000-$73,000 a year), exceeds the wage rise (~$65,000), and dwarfs the finance-cost increase (~$3,000-$4,000). Unlike wages, timber cannot be re-spread across fewer hours, and TSF's advertised 10% introductory discount already narrows room to lift prices. TSF should lock in forward timber contracts, renegotiate the 10% discount tiers, and pass a measured surcharge to academy contracts to protect the $12.00 contribution.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to TSF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TSF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of TSF with a well-justified judgement that timber input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
